# ya-runtime-vm 0.6.0

Version 0.6.0 replaces the external QEMU runtime with embedded OpenVMM and a
Rust guest agent communicating over virtio-vsock. It promotes the validated
v0.6.0-rc5 implementation without further runtime code changes.

## Changes

- Boot Linux directly with KVM on Linux hosts or Windows Hypervisor Platform
  (WHP) on Windows hosts. Packages include the guest kernel and initramfs.
- Preserve stdout and stderr through process completion, including large output
  and small cyclic buffers, and handle entrypoint completion and guest shutdown.
- Share host directories through virtio-fs with filename validation, pinned
  host handles, and per-share logical byte and entry budgets.
- Enable selected, host-supported KVM paravirtual features for clocks,
  interrupt handling, spinlocks, TLB flush, IPIs and scheduling. Require KVM to
  enforce the advertised feature policy on every ordinary guest vCPU.
- Include static Linux musl, Windows MSVC and Debian packages with license
  notices and SHA-256 checksums.

## Compatibility

Linux hosts require access to `/dev/kvm` and support for
`KVM_CAP_ENFORCE_PV_FEATURE_CPUID`. Startup fails if enforcement is unavailable
or cannot be enabled. With nested virtualization, this requirement applies
to the Linux kernel running the runtime inside the provider VM.

Native Windows uses WHP and does not require this KVM capability. Enable
Windows Hypervisor Platform before running the runtime.

Temporary storage uses raw disk images instead of qcow2; existing temporary
qcow2 data is not compatible. GPU passthrough is outside this release's scope.

## Validation

The rc5 release passed Linux and Windows native checks, the RustSec audit,
Linux KVM integration tests, packaging and checksum verification. The stable
release repeats these checks before publication. Local direct-host and nested
KVM tests also passed, including concurrent guest probes of PV restrictions.

Actual Windows WHP guest execution remains unverified. These tests do not
establish long-duration workload reliability or a general startup speedup
over QEMU. KVM PV enforcement restricts feature-gated operations; it is not a
general MSR or hypercall firewall.
